in writing. ‒ i supported the 2014 annual report of the european investment bank (eib). the eib investment programme supports the policy objectives of the european union and prioritises investments aimed at accelerating recovery and increasing productivity. the report also pays particular attention to promoting youth employment, increasing the share of innovation and incentives for smes. the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 264 concerning the establishment of a european data protection supervisor. the report also encourages the eib to continue investing in education, skills development and jobs for young people, and details improvements in environmental sustainability and climate action, the promotion of economic and social cohesion and convergence, the management of the european fund for strategic investments (efsi), and many others.
in writing. ‒ the european investment bank (eib) provides financial support for projects of union interest, thereby contributing to the balanced development of the internal market and to social, economic and territorial cohesion. on the positive side, in 2014 the eib financed 285 000 smes, safeguarding 3,6 million jobs. the eib should further promote job creation and growth in the eu. the eib currently conceals the identity of the final beneficiaries or beneficial owners of co-financed projects. in addition, it finances projects through intermediaries using tax havens or companies with aggressive tax planning. it is necessary for the eib to strengthen its activities in the field of transparency, thereby improving the quality of information on final beneficiaries. the report highlights the fight against tax evasion, but also puts the emphasis on transparency and the fight against fraud and corruption. the eib has to stop disbursements under loans to projects that are subject to national/european investigations for suspected corruption. another important aspect of the report is the environment and sustainable production. the 13 new member states received only 1% of the funding for renewable energy capacity development. the report calls for the promotion of new investments in environmentally friendly and sustainable production and for a gradual increase in the share of investments in the new member states. that's why i supported the report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the european investment bank (eib) annual report 2014. i welcome the call for the european investment bank to provide more technical support to member states with a lower project approval rate in the pre-approval phase and encourage it to facilitate the exchange of best practice examples between member states in relation to the successful preparation of calls for projects. the european investment bank must also focus on investing in the real economy to boost job creation and growth in the eu.
in writing. ‒ report on the european investment bank (eib) i have endorsed the 2014 annual report, having regard to the 2014 activity report of the european investment bank (eib), the 2014 eib financial report and the 2014 eib statistical report. the eib's main task as an eu bank is to provide financial support for projects of eu interest which contribute to the balanced development of the internal market and social, economic and territorial cohesion, thus strengthening european integration, which is essential to boosting the eu's competitiveness, in addition to employment. in 2014, the eib financed 285 000 smes, safeguarding 3.6 million jobs, and signed contracts for a total of 413 projects within the eu worth eur 69 billion and 92 new projects outside the eu for a total of eur 7.98 billion.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the european investment bank (eib) for the financial year 2014, which presented credibly the achievements. the eib financed 285 000 smes in 2014, safeguarding 3.6 million jobs, among other things. the eib's main task as an eu bank is therefore to provide financial support for projects of union interest which contribute to the balanced development of the internal market and to social, economic and territorial cohesion, thereby strengthening european integration and contributing to greater employment and competitiveness in the union.
in writing. ‒ i supported the motion for a resolution on attacks on hospitals and schools in armed attacks around the world. the resolution expresses the view that investigations into such acts should be conducted independently and that all criminals involved should be held accountable and all participants in such crimes should be dealt with. health and education workers, humanitarian organisations must be involved in the rehabilitation of patients and children, while at the same time providing medical assistance to the family members of victims. the resolution also recognises the importance and the unique nature of the european union guidelines on the promotion and respect of international humanitarian law, as no other country or international organisation has adopted an equivalent document to date.
in writing. ‒ the international community has witnessed an unrelenting trend of attacks on hospitals and schools in armed conflicts around the world over the past few years, such as the recent attacks on doctors without borders (msf) health centres in kunduz, afghanistan, on 3 october 2015, in raza, yemen, on 10 january 2016, and in many syrian conflict towns. the resolution condemns attacks on hospitals and schools as prohibited under international law and recognises that such acts constitute grave breaches of the 1949 geneva conventions and war crimes under the rome statute of the international criminal court. member states and eu institutions are called upon to recognise the real scale of these emergencies and to use all the means at their disposal to address them. respect international humanitarian law and ensure that health and educational institutions are neutral and their premises protected in times of armed conflict. transparent, independent and impartial investigations into brutal attacks are needed. i therefore voted in favour of the report and therefore supported it in the plenary.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the joint motion for a resolution on attacks on hospitals and schools as violations of international humanitarian law. i welcome the invitation to the member states of the european union to take the opportunity of the world humanitarian summit to reaffirm the central importance of international humanitarian law and the protection it provides. international humanitarian law has made a decisive contribution to modern human history. the use and attacks on hospitals and schools by participants in armed conflicts are reprehensible.
in writing. ‒ i supported the resolution on attacks on hospitals and schools as violations of international humanitarian law. the international community has witnessed a horrifying trend in recent years of attacks on hospitals and schools in armed conflicts around the world, most recently on médecins sans frontières (msf) health centres. we are witnessing the most extensive denial and prevention of humanitarian aid, the killing of civilians and humanitarian workers, detention in extremely poor conditions, and the taking of hostages and the forced enslavement of civilians. the current humanitarian system has reached its limits, forcing many organisations to suspend food aid, shelter and other life-saving humanitarian operations. it is necessary to strengthen the protection of humanitarian workers and to ensure the same level of security measures for international and local staff.
in writing. ‒ the increasing number of non-state actors, terrorist groups and other actors in armed conflicts is making it more difficult to implement international humanitarian law. there are worrying reports of deadly attacks on hospitals, schools and other civilian targets, which are increasingly common during armed conflicts around the world, and in which the targets and victims are patients, students, medical and educational staff, humanitarian workers, children and family members entities that are particularly protected by international law.
in writing. ‒ the right of access to eu documents is guaranteed by the treaty on the functioning of the european union (article 15) and by the charter of fundamental rights of the european union (article 42). the mechanisms for submitting requests for documents and the rules on exceptions are developed in regulation 1049/2001 on access to parliament, council and commission documents the eu equivalent of access to information and freedom to provide legal advice. transparent administration is in the interests of citizens, the fight against corruption and the legitimacy of the political system and union law. however, the institutions, agencies and other bodies of the european union are unfortunately not yet fully complying with the rules and changes envisaged by the lisbon treaty and the charter of fundamental rights in the application of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001, in particular as regards participatory democracy. the eu must take further steps to increase the transparency of its governance and its legislative process. the main aspects covered by the report are: transparency and democracy, transparency of the legislative process, mandatory lobby register and international agreements. for the reasons stated above, i supported the report and voted in favour of its adoption.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on public access to documents (rule 116 (7) of the rules of procedure) in 2014 and 2015. the three institutions did not take appropriate follow-up to many of the recommendations in the resolution on public access to documents for 2011-2013, which is a matter of concern. it is also regrettable that the eu institutions and bodies have not designated a transparency officer within their governance structure, who would be responsible for compliance and improving practices. i urge the institutions to do so as soon as possible.
in writing. ‒ i supported the report on public access to documents (rule 116 (7) of the rules of procedure) in 2014 and 2015. full transparency is the basis for citizens' trust in the eu institutions, contributes to an understanding of the rights deriving from the union acquis and to awareness and knowledge of the eu decision-making process, including the proper implementation of administrative and legislative procedures. the right of access to documents is a fundamental right protected by the charter of fundamental rights and the treaties and transposed into national law by regulation (ec) no 1049/2001.
in writing. ‒ i supported the report on public access to documents in 2014 and 2015 because it gives a credible picture of the situation. the right of access to documents is a fundamental right protected by the charter of fundamental rights and the treaties and its exercise needs to be monitored at all times. i believe that the eu institutions must operate in their activities and policies on the basis of representative democracy, as laid down in article 10 (1) teu, and thus ensure that the principles of full transparency, sharing and correct and timely information of citizens are respected.
in writing. ‒ i also supported the report on domestic workers and carers in the european union, as i believe it raises a number of topical issues. it should be noted that both very large categories of domestic workers and carers are dominated by women, who are predominantly immigrants. they usually have a low level of education and need to work to support themselves and their families, but in doing so they often lack the appropriate contracts with employers and, consequently, lack social rights. the report therefore makes a clear call for all member states to contribute to the promotion and protection of human rights and to strongly condemn all forms of abuse, harassment and violence against all workers, and in particular domestic workers. i also supported the report because it contains a recommendation to member states to launch awareness campaigns to raise awareness among public and private bodies, families and the general public, so that these professions are properly recognised and recognised.
in writing. ‒ in 2010, 2.5 million people were employed in the eu in the domestic work sector, 88% of whom were women, as this sector is characterised by feminization. the report calls for the introduction of a general framework for the professionalisation of domestic workers and carers in the eu. unfortunately, both sectors are rife with illegal work and exploitation of workers. professionalisation confers on workers in a particular sector the same employment and social protection rights as employees with a statutory contract. the commission is invited to propose a directive on carer's leave and a framework for the recognition of the status of non-professional carers, who will be guaranteed a salary and minimum standards of social protection during the period in which they carry out caring tasks. it also calls on the commission and the member states to ensure the availability of legal migration routes to the eu and to put in place targeted programmes for legal migration. there is a need to introduce measures that can improve the living and working conditions of domestic workers and carers in the eu, which is why i supported the report.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the report on domestic workers and carers in the eu. we need a common recognition at european union level of the profession and the value of domestic and care work as genuine work, as recognition of this professional sector is likely to reduce the volume of undeclared work and promote social inclusion. the european union and the member states must establish common rules for domestic and care work. it is also necessary to prepare a set of policy instruments, both legislative and non-legislative, for domestic work.
in writing. ‒ i abstained in the vote on the report on domestic workers and carers in the eu. household work, in which the majority of workers are women, provides favourable conditions for the exploitation of workers. such exploitation constitutes a serious violation of fundamental rights, from which both undocumented workers and eu citizens need to be protected. more than a third of domestic workers are not entitled to maternity leave and related rights and benefits. in some member states, domestic workers and carers are not entitled to unemployment benefit. the financial and social crisis and the austerity measures implemented in the eu have taken a heavy toll on its citizens and residents, increasing job insecurity, poverty, unemployment and social exclusion, and leading to limited or no access to public services and social protection services. by professionalizing the profession of housewife, women would be granted full rights as employees under an employment contract. it would also go into another area that we've been avoiding for a long time and reduce the amount of black-ops. regulation in this area would not only benefit individuals who receive social security but also society as a whole.
in writing. ‒ i abstained from the vote on the report on domestic workers and carers in the eu. i agree that the area of domestic and care workers in the eu member states is unregulated and needs to be reformed, but this area falls within the competence of the member states.
in writing. ‒ i supported the european parliament's motion for a resolution on gender equality and the empowerment of women in the digital age. i believe that the potential of the information society, information and communication technologies and the internet to promote the empowerment of women, their rights and freedoms and gender equality should be fully exploited. and this is regardless of circumstances such as age, disability, genetic characteristics, gender, race, social or ethical background, or economic status. the internet has become a key tool for the daily lives of individuals in family, professional, study and learning environments, for management in companies, public authorities, institutions and organisations, and for the functioning of social networks and the promotion of equal opportunities. i am convinced that its benefits can be used even more effectively, including in promoting gender equality.
in writing. i supported a report that addresses the challenges of digitalisation, which has radically changed the way people access information, communicate, socialise, study and work. digitalisation creates new opportunities for participation in public and political debates, education and the labour market, opens up new possibilities for self-determination and has a great economic potential for the european union and for countries outside it, and impacts on society as a whole. the information society offers great opportunities for creation and development and a great potential for the empowerment of women, so it is important to use the instruments of the digital agenda and the digital single market strategy and to make them more targeted, to close the large gender gap in the ict sector and to promote the full inclusion of women in the sector.
in writing. - digitalisation has changed our lives. we have better access to information, different ways of socializing, studying and working. new opportunities for participation in public and political debates, and for participation in education and the labour market, are being created, representing a great economic potential for the european union. unfortunately, it turns out that there is a huge gender gap in the digital sector. while digitalisation is increasing and has a strong impact on the labour market and on society as a whole, women still have difficulties accessing the ict (information and communication technologies) sector, where they represent only 30% of the workforce. efforts should be made to address this persistent gender imbalance and further efforts should be made to reduce gender gaps in the ict sector. this can be achieved through targeted policy actions to tackle gender stereotypes and mainstream the principle of gender equality in all the european commission's digital initiatives, as well as through targeted investments that promote equality in the digital sector. women are an important resource for the european economy. equal participation of women in the ict sector would mean an annual gain of around eur 9 billion for eu gdp. women and girls must be at the forefront of the digital single market strategy, which is why i voted in favour of the report and therefore supported it.
in writing. ‒ i supported the report on gender equality and the empowerment of women in the digital age. digitalisation has radically changed the way people access and provide information, communicate, socialize, study and work, creating new opportunities for participation in public and political debates, education and the labour market, opening up new possibilities for self-determination and having great economic potential for the european union and for countries outside it. digitalisation affects not only markets but also society as a whole.
member of the commission.– madam president, regarding cohesion policy in mountainous regions, the commission welcomes ms iotova’s report and notes the call for cohesion policy to address the specific challenges faced by mountainous regions. the european structural and investment funds (esif) have a long tradition of supporting regions with specific geographical features, which includes mountain regions. the esif regulation already provides several possibilities to take account of the situation of mountainous regions, such as the modulation of co-financing rates and the use of the new territorial tools, that is: community-led local development and integrated territorial investments. the esif support programmes and strategies specifically targeting mountainous regions have introduced tools for integrated strategies, such as the eu macro-regional strategy for the alpine region. the commission will ask in its monitoring and review meetings with the member states how they address the specific situation of mountain regions and how the possibilities offered by the esif regulations have been taken up. it is therefore important to make the most of what the current regulation has to offer, such as the new territorial development tools which i have just mentioned. regarding the new territorial development tools in cohesion policy: as underlined in ms tomašić’s report, integrated territorial investment and community-led local development are decisive for the involvement of local and regional actors. the commission strongly believes that the introduction of these new territorial tools has been a significant step forward in promoting an integrated place-based approach to territorial development. i would like to underline that a significant amount of guidance has been provided to member states and to local actors, both on integrated territorial investment and on community-led local development, to promote the use of these tools. the commission will continue its strong efforts to share information and share best practices, both with member states as well as with local actors. these efforts translate the commission’s willingness to assist member states in ensuring quality implementation of cohesion policy. finally, regarding the oral question. with a budget of more than eur 450 billion and over eur 215 billion for cohesion policy for 2014-2020, the european structural and investment funds are europe’s main investment policy tools. to maximise their impact, a reformed cohesion policy framework was advocated and adopted in agreement with the member states. this framework puts the emphasis on the results, which concentrated funding on priority teams and areas, and investments based on good strategic planning. the reformed cohesion policy requires good quality implementation subsequent to proper programming, planning and preparatory work. due to considerable joint efforts with member states, the commission adopted half of the cohesion policy programmes already in the course of 2014, in spite of delays in adoption of the regulatory framework. however, under shared management, actual implementation of the programmes is the responsibility of the member states. the commission notes that designations of programme authorities took place for less than one quarter of programmes. furthermore, the number of payment claims received is still low. member states are strongly encouraged to continue and to intensify their efforts and there is scope for political pressure in this regard. the commission provided targeted assistance for eight member states covered under the task force for better implementation initiative, reducing significantly the risk of decommitment of funds at closure for the 2007—2013 period to below eur 5 billion, just over one per cent. the targeted approach, centred on member states and programmes at risk of implementation, continues in 2014-2020, and that includes closure-related tasks. our starting point for discussions with member states on the funding priorities was rooted in three pillars: the europe 2020 targets; the relevant country-specific recommendations; and the socio-economic analysis at member state and regional level. in the coming years, future country-specific recommendations may trigger, where relevant, esif programme adjustments. these can also be triggered at the initiative of the commission, ensuring the commission’s support for structural reforms in member states. regarding administrative capacity, to which the 2014-2020 regulations have dedicated a thematic objective with a specific allocation, the commission will continue to assist member states, including through the newly-established structural reform support service, in carrying out structural reforms in line with the european semester process and the country-specific recommendations. furthermore, member states can speed up implementation without losing the quality of the spending by using the expanded range of simplified cost options in the 2014-2020 regulatory framework. the reduction in administrative burden this brings about will ensure a more rapid reimbursement of funds, with a greater focus on the results and a lower risk of errors as compared to reimbursement on the basis of real costs. regarding automatic decommitment of funds in the third year following commitment, this should be less of a concern in 2014-2020. according to current assumptions, no significant decommitments are expected in this period. this is due to the generic application of the three-year rule instead of the two-year rule across all member states and to the annual refinancing payments made to the member states. nevertheless, timely implementation of the cohesion policy allocation is crucial to avoid an accumulation of payment applications towards the end of the programming period and, first and foremost, to ensure that programmes deliver results on the ground as early as possible.

in writing. ‒ i supported the report on new territorial development tools in cohesion policy for the period 2014-2020. the treaty of lisbon recognised territorial cohesion as a fundamental objective in the development of the european union. the european structural and investment funds (esif) frameworks present two new tools for achieving territorial cohesion, namely integrated territorial investment and local community development. the adoption of the report laid the foundations for the implementation of both new tools, both at the implementation level and in the early stages of the implementation of cohesion policy for the period 2014-2020.
in writing. ‒ territorial cohesion is considered a fundamental objective of the european union and is enshrined in the lisbon treaty. accordingly, the new generation of cohesion policy for the 2014-2020 programming period places more emphasis on the use of integrated and local approaches to promote economic, social and territorial cohesion, including the introduction of two new instruments: community-led local development and integrated territorial investment. community-led local development follows a bottom-up approach, meaning that objectives and funded projects are determined on the basis of local community needs rather than imposed at national level. it is crucial that local partners take the lead in the preparation of the territorial development strategy for integrated territorial investments and are fully involved in its management, monitoring and audit. territorial integrated investments, on the other hand, are an instrument that allows for a more flexible definition of the territorial scope and thus the application of a genuinely local approach. the report calls for these instruments to be strengthened and made mandatory, if necessary, for the period after 2020. the report also takes account of the greens' efforts to demand high standards from local actors, and highlights the importance of local ownership, tackling youth unemployment and demographic challenges. i supported the report because of the above.

in writing. ‒ the production of reliable statistics on balance of payments, international trade in services and foreign direct investment is important for monitoring the main features of economic development, such as changes in current accounts and financial flows within and outside the eu. these statistics contribute to ensuring that member states' economic policies are consistent with the eu's broader guidelines and legal requirements, and also provide an important basis for monitoring macroeconomic imbalance processes. the report includes additional legal requirements to increase transparency and disaggregation of balance of payments, international trade in services and foreign direct investment, as well as to take advantage of legal innovations such as the newly created register of final beneficiaries. the statistics should also allow for a distinction to be made between direct investment in new projects and direct investment in take-overs that do not increase gross investments in the member states. the report also envisages that the european commission will have to carry out pilot studies if it is to develop a methodology for collecting these statistics within the three-year timeframe envisaged. in short, the report contributes to improving the transparency of eu statistics on balance of payments, international trade in services and foreign direct investment, which is why i supported it.

in writing. ‒ i supported the proposal for a regulation regulating exemptions for merchants. the term 'commodity trader' covers a wide range of actors in the energy and primary products markets. the requirements laid down in the capital requirements regulation and the capital requirements directive apply to both credit institutions and investment firms. the capital requirements regulation exempts merchants engaged in the provision of investment services or activities in relation to financial instruments from the requirements for large exposures and capital requirements respectively. as both exemptions expire at the end of 2017, the commission decided to undertake a single review of the legal framework for merchants and the prudential supervision of investment firms in general, which will ensure the development of a harmonised prudential framework for all types of investment firms. in the absence of a specific credit rating framework that could be established through the review of investment firms by the end of 2017, all requirements of the capital requirements regulation and the capital requirements directive will apply to merchants from the beginning of 2018.
in writing. ‒ articles of the capital requirements regulation exempt merchants from the requirements for large exposures and capital requirements respectively. both exemptions expired on 31 december 2017. this self-derogation clause was initially included in the capital requirements regulation in order to provide regulators with sufficient time to establish a prudential regime adapted to the risk profile of merchants. commodity traders include a wide range of players in the energy and primary products markets. the commission decided to carry out a single review of the relevant arrangements for merchants and the prudential supervision of investment firms in general and to prepare a joint report on the above issues. but because it's a complex project, it won't be finished by the end of this year. therefore, it is unlikely that legislation resulting from this review would be prepared, adopted and implemented before the expiry of the current exemptions, meaning that merchants would be subject to all the requirements of the capital requirements regulation and the capital requirements directive from then on. in order to avoid such a situation, it is appropriate to extend the validity of the existing exemptions provided for in the capital requirements regulation. that is why i voted for the report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending the regulation on exemptions for traders in goods. the exemptions from the capital requirements regulation that exempt merchants from the large exposures and capital requirements will expire at the end of 2017 and therefore require an amendment to the regulation. otherwise, merchants would be subject to all the requirements of the cr and crd. without a conscious (and informed) decision that such treatment is indeed the most appropriate for them, and assuming that the review of investment firms would result in a prudential framework adapted to commodity traders, they would be deprived of a stable regulatory framework.

on behalf of the s&d group. the fact is that the european schengen system has been put at risk by the migrant crisis. in view of the recent developments, coreper has today adopted the european commission's proposal to extend border controls at internal schengen borders for a further six months. it is true that in some areas these boundaries are still fragile and that the situation is not yet fully and definitively stabilised. but the situation is far from alarming. it seems more likely that the reasons for this extension are questionable. we cannot accept the principle of extending internal controls simply 'to stock' and at the discretion of individual members. this creates additional internal tension, also between the new and old members of the union, which we absolutely do not need at this moment. nor do we need to exploit border control changes for political campaigning, as austria recently did by sending in the military to an otherwise empty border crossing. the creation of such a frightening situation and the seeming fight against an invisible enemy send a very bad signal to the citizens of europe. however, we must insist that the commission should report as soon as possible after the introduction of the extension of internal border controls on whether and to what extent this measure is proportionate. it should also do so in the light of the fact that the introduction of border controls in some member states has paralysed the transport and logistics sector across europe and that the consequences of these controls will generate between eur 5 and 18 billion in direct costs annually, in particular in road and freight transport, as well as in tourism and cross-border mobility. instead of isolating member states - which will not prevent internal terrorist attacks by european citizens - we must focus our forces and resources on ensuring the effective functioning of the schengen external border and on helping countries that still face high migratory pressures.

in writing. ‒ crossborder tax avoidance, aggressive tax planning and harmful tax competition are increasingly challenging for the eu. we need more transparency on tax information to prevent aggressive tax planning, in particular by introducing reporting for multinational groups by individual countries. the current legal framework does not yet require member states to provide reports to other eu member states, which would require increased transparency. multinationals based or operating in the eu with total consolidated revenues of eur 750 million or more will be required to report on a country-by-country basis. the competent authority of the member state receiving this report shall, by automatic exchange, forward it to all other member states in which one or more entities within a multinational group are resident for tax purposes or taxable in respect of activities carried out through a permanent establishment of the group. the greens were critical of the limitation of the reporting obligations to the largest companies generating more than eur 750 million in annual revenue, as the commission has thus significantly reduced the volume of companies covered by the measures. although our proposals to lower this threshold were not accepted, it is still a step forward compared to the previous situation, and i supported the report at the meeting.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the proposal for a council directive amending the directive on the mandatory automatic exchange of information in the field of taxation. i support the amendment of the directive which, inter alia, with regard to the use of aggressive tax planning practices by multinational companies, which are not available to domestic companies, emphasises that in addition to the significant harm to smes, it also leads to distortions and irregularities in the functioning of the internal market and to distortions of competition to the detriment of smes. i also welcome the proposal for an amendment to the directive which adds that it is essential for the eu to design tax rules in such a way that they do not jeopardise growth or investment, do not put union companies at a competitive disadvantage and do not increase the risk of double taxation of companies.
in writing. ‒ i supported the report on the proposal for a council directive amending directive 2011/16/eu as regards the mandatory automatic exchange of information in the field of taxation, as it represents a positive step towards combating aggressive tax planning systems. in the future, further safeguards will need to be adopted to ensure that competition in the single market is not distorted by favourable national tax deals with multinationals. the proposal is an important step in the fight against unfair tax practices in eu countries, as it aims to increase transparency and reduce harmful tax competition. the european commission must have full access to the information exchanged between the tax authorities of the member states in order to assess whether their tax practices comply with european rules.
in writing. ‒ in recent years, the challenge posed by tax fraud, tax avoidance and tax evasion has increased significantly and is a major concern for the union and globally. i supported the report as i agree that automatic exchange of data is an important tool for ensuring a future european and international standard of transparency and exchange of data in tax matters. however, i believe that it is essential for the union that tax rules are designed in such a way that they do not jeopardise growth or investment, do not put union companies at a competitive disadvantage and do not increase the risk of double taxation of companies, and should also minimise their costs and administrative burden.
in writing. ‒ last year, a study was carried out in brussels, including in restaurants within the european institutions, on the appropriateness of the labelling of fish dishes. the international non-governmental organization oceana used dna testing to identify fish prepared in restaurants and to compare the findings with claims made by vendors about the dishes served. in more than 30 percent of the dishes analysed, the claims made by the vendors regarding the fish used in the preparation of the dish did not correspond to the results of the dna tests. ngos have reached similar conclusions elsewhere. although regulation (eu) no 1169/2011 contains a provision on consumer information on food, including sales in restaurants, member states delegate their responsibility for requiring food providers to comply with the provision appropriately. i believe that the debate on the traceability of fishery and aquaculture products in restaurants and retail sales would contribute to ensuring proper labelling in restaurants in the future, which is why i supported the resolution at the meeting.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on the question for oral answer on the traceability of fishery and aquaculture products in restaurants and retail outlets. some studies indicate that there is a significant prevalence of incorrect labelling of fishery products sold on the eu market, including in restaurants of eu institutions, in breach of eu regulations, including the rules of the common fisheries policy, which may be considered a criminal offence under national law. i support stronger controls by member states and an effective fight against fraud.
in writing. ‒ motions for resolutions - i supported the traceability of fishery and aquaculture products in restaurants and retail outlets, as there is a need for greater transparency and traceability in the labelling of fishery and aquaculture products in restaurants and retail outlets. 70% of fishery and aquaculture products on the european market are imported, so it is important that they meet the same standards as european products. the european people's party has for many years been advocating a single european food label that would ensure respect for environmental, social and health standards.
in writing. ‒ the eu is the world's largest seafood market, backed by products from its fishing sector and imports from third countries. however, various studies have found that intentional and fraudulent mislabelling of fishery products sold on the eu market is frequent. i therefore voted in favour of a european parliament resolution on the traceability of fishery and aquaculture products in restaurants and retail outlets and the introduction of a reliable traceability system from landing to consumption, in order to ensure consumer confidence and consequently reduce dependence on imported fishery and aquaculture products, thereby strengthening the eu market.
in writing. ‒ china is not a classical market economy, and i therefore supported the motion for a resolution on eu-china trade relations and market economy status, which points to shortcomings in china's fulfilment of the conditions for acquiring market economy status. as long as china does not meet the five criteria set by the eu to define market economies, the non-standard methodology for establishing price comparability should be used for the anti-dumping investigations of chinese imports. the commission must take due account of the concerns expressed by our members about the industrial sector in the eu and ensure the protection of european jobs, the environment, standards and sustainable economic growth. the consequences of the chinese overcapacity are already manifested in the detrimental effect on the eu steel industry, which already has visible social consequences. but i will not oppose the granting of market economy status to china when the conditions are met and when it does not pose such a high risk to the european economy.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the resolution on china's market economy status. the european parliament must play a key role and its role must not be undermined. the strategic partnership between the european union and china must be equal and fair and based on fair trade relations. it should also aim at improving standards in the field of human and labour rights.
in writing. ‒ i supported the motion for a resolution on china's market economy status, as china does not yet meet the european union's conditions for obtaining market economy status. the european commission must listen to the concerns of eu industry and trade unions about the potential consequences for the environment, jobs and economic growth of china's market economy status. at the same time, we must not forget the importance of our partnership with china, the eu's second largest trading partner with a daily trade volume of over €1 billion.
in writing. ‒ i supported the european parliament's resolution on the status of china as a market economy. china is the eu's second largest trading partner, with daily trade flows between them well in excess of eur 1 billion. china's overproduction already has major social, economic and environmental consequences in the eu. i therefore believe that a comprehensive reform of the eu's trade defence instruments is urgently needed, which fully respects wto rules and ensures that european industry is placed on a level playing field with china and other trading partners.
in writing. ‒ i supported the motion for a resolution on the follow-up to and review of the 2030 agenda. the 2030 agenda for sustainable development establishes a global framework for eradicating poverty and achieving sustainable development by 2030, and builds on the millennium development goals adopted in 2000. it is the first global agreement to set out a universal and comprehensive plan of action and includes an ambitious set of 17 overarching sustainable development goals. the agenda sets out clearly the guidelines for sustainable development based on peace and justice. i would also point out that the eu is one of the communities of un member states that adheres quite consistently to the agenda's guidelines - after all, the eu is the world's largest donor of humanitarian aid. unfortunately, this cannot be said for some other, more developed, un member states.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution at the end of the debate on the council and commission statements on the follow-up to and review of the 2030 agenda. the 2030 agenda and the sustainable development goals commit the international community to eradicating poverty and redefine and update our development strategies for the next 15 years. i support the call for the foreign affairs council to adopt a common position of the european union, in line with parliament's position, on the next steps and the current state of play of the 2030 agenda and the sustainable development goals. this is essential for the eu's credibility and leadership.
in writing. ‒ i supported the motion for a resolution on the next steps and state of play of the 2030 agenda and the sdgs, as the proposed package of 230 sdg indicators is a good starting point and a solid framework for the next steps and review of progress towards the 17 sdgs. the focus is on the international commitment to eradicate poverty, redefine and update our development strategies for the next 15 years and deliver results.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the joint resolution on the 2030 agenda, which sets out a global framework for eradicating poverty and achieving sustainable development by 2030, and builds on the millennium development goals adopted in 2000. it is the first global agreement to set out a universal and comprehensive plan of action, based on a global partnership involving action by governments and stakeholders at all levels. the european union has played a leading role in this process from the outset, as by far the world's largest donor of development aid. i believe that the new eu sustainable development strategy and its related implementing measures should be widely consulted by all stakeholders, including national parliaments, local authorities and civil society, on the basis of an inclusive process.
in writing. ‒ i supported the european parliament's motion for a resolution on the mandatory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance for certain foods. according to a 2013 eurobarometer survey, 84% of consumers believe that the country of origin should be indicated on milk, whether it is liquid milk or dairy products. a commission report of 17 december 2013 showed that 90% of consumers want to know the origin of processed meat in food. the resolution welcomes the eurobarometer findings and calls for mandatory origin labelling of meat other than beef, pig, sheep, goat or poultry meat, milk, milk used as an ingredient in dairy products, unprocessed foods, single ingredient products and ingredients representing more than 50% of a food. the commission has also proposed that the eu should be able to provide the union with a comprehensive list of the countries that are eligible for the scheme. i hope that this time the commission will take our warning and the consumer's warning seriously.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament has already adopted several resolutions on the issue of the indication of the country of origin of foodstuffs. for example, in its resolution on meat in processed foods adopted on 11 february 2015, parliament called on the european commission to prepare a legislative proposal to introduce mandatory indication of the country of origin of meat in processed foods. although this would ensure greater transparency in the food chain and also improve the information of european consumers, the european commission has not yet made such a proposal. the resolution calls on the commission to make the indication of the country of origin or place of provenance compulsory for all types of milk, milk products and meat products for human consumption, which is a very important requirement. it also includes an invitation to the commission to submit legislative proposals to make the indication of the origin of meat in processed foods compulsory. the resolution also stresses that the labelling of origin is not enough in itself, but that a stronger approach to monitoring and enforcement of the law and to introducing stricter penalties for infringers is also needed. i agree that the european commission should draw up legislative proposals for the labelling of food origin, which would also restore consumer confidence in food, and i therefore supported the resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the motion for a resolution on the oral question on the mandatory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance for certain foods. the motion for a resolution is populist and therefore i could not support it. it also claims, inter alia, that the mandatory indication of the origin of milk sold as such or used as an ingredient in milk products is a useful measure to protect the quality of milk products and to combat food fraud, which is absolutely not true. the horse meat affair made this clear, as the meat had markings, but it was a fraudulent marking.
in writing. ‒ i supported the european parliament resolution of 12 may 2016 on the mandatory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance for certain foods (2016/2583 ((rsp)). mandatory labelling would give consumers greater confidence in food products and at the same time make the food supply more transparent. the country of origin labels could mean more competitiveness for slovenian suppliers on the eu market, as our products are considered to be of higher quality.
in writing. ‒ i did not support the resolution calling on the commission to make the indication of the country of origin or place of provenance compulsory for all types of milk, milk products and meat products for consumption, and to submit legislative proposals to make the indication of the origin of meat in processed foods compulsory. i think that the resolution fails to take account of some important aspects. the introduction of compulsory designation of origin could lead to the renationalisation of the european internal market. it also ignores the fact that the higher price due to the additional designation of origin imposes an additional financial burden on farmers and poorer households.
in writing. ‒ i supported the motion for a european parliament resolution on the application of council directive 2010/18/eu of 8 march 2010 implementing the revised framework agreement on parental leave concluded between the confederation of european large enterprises (businesseurope), the european association of craftsmen and small businesses (ueapme), the european association of enterprises and employees in public services (ceep) and the european trade union confederation (etuc). the europe 2020 strategy sets the target of 75% employment rate for both sexes. this target has already been reached for men, while there is a strong likelihood that for women, where the employment rate is currently 63.5%, the target will most likely not be met by 2020. the agreement adopted therefore calls for the adoption of comprehensive measures to increase the participation of women in the labour market, in particular through a package of policies to equally distribute family and household activities, child rearing and care for other dependants between men and women. i would also mention that slovenia is at the top of the european ranking in terms of maternity and parental leave, due to the length of leave and the balanced distribution between the sexes.
in writing. ‒ the european union has adopted two pieces of legislation on family leave in recent decades, namely on maternity and parental leave, which are relatively old and adopted on a different legal basis. the report sends a clear message to the european commission and the eu member states to step up their efforts to further improve the conditions for parental leave. workers on parental leave should be entitled to adequate financial compensation and should be supported in their return to the labour market. although specific support is provided for paternity leave, it would make more sense to make parental leave rights non-transferable. i believe that the eu should develop a comprehensive package of measures on parental leave in the coming months, as a well-regulated parental leave would contribute to the work-life balance of workers. the report pays particular attention to the link between parental leave and women's labour market participation, as well as to paternity leave and its lack of use. such a report is required by an eu directive introducing a mandatory two-week paternity leave. although the report on the application of council directive 2010/18/eu does not call for a revision of the maternity leave directive, i believe it is a step in the right direction and that is why i supported it.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the application of the council directive of 8 march 2010 implementing the revised framework agreement on parental leave concluded between businesseurope, ueapme, ceep and etuc and repealing directive 96/34/ec. the transposition of provisions adopted in different forms in the member states must be carried out in full respect of the current legislation in the field of collective bargaining between the social partners. since the commission has withdrawn its proposal to amend the maternity leave directive, i support the call for it to re-formulate an ambitious proposal, respecting the principle of subsidiarity, which will actually allow for a better reconciliation of work and private life.
in writing. ‒ i supported the european parliament resolution of 12 may 2016 on the application of council directive 2010/18/eu of 8 march 2010 implementing the revised framework agreement on parental leave concluded between businesseurope, ueapme, ceep and etuc and repealing directive 96/34/ec. within the eu, there are wide differences in parental leave, notably in terms of who is entitled to it. more european commission monitoring is needed on the implementation of the rules, with a focus on gender non-discrimination in the right to parental leave. member states should ensure that the right to parental leave is accessible to all, while encouraging fathers to exercise this right as well. a proposal was also made to extend unpaid parental leave from 4 months to 6 months.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the implementation of the revised framework agreement on parental leave, which stresses that the reconciliation of work and private life is a fundamental right of the individual and must be taken into account in the development of labour legislation. eurostat data for 2010 show that 3 518 600 people took parental leave, of whom only 94 800 (2.7%) were men. the gender gap in employment, according to eurofound research, represents a serious loss for the european economy, amounting to approximately eur 370 billion in 2013. the european commission, together with the member states, should take specific measures for the new organisation of work with more flexible models. these measures would help to reduce discrimination against women and enable them to enter and remain in the labour market and to return to it without economic and social pressure.
in writing. ‒ i supported the motion for a resolution on the implementation of the directive on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and the protection of its victims in the context of gender equality, as it provides for better protection of victims of trafficking in human beings and reduces the opportunities for potential victims. there is insufficient attention to trafficking in certain vulnerable groups such as young people, the homeless, children and the disabled. this is especially true in the face of the current refugee crisis and the alarming number of missing children in europe. therefore, data collection needs to be improved in order to identify more victims from these groups and to develop best practices in addressing their specific needs. the eu institutions must closely assess the implementation of eu law in the member states and take further legislative or other action as necessary to improve efforts to combat trafficking in human beings.
in writing. ‒ trafficking in human beings constitutes a violation of fundamental human rights as enshrined in article 5 of the eu charter of fundamental rights and a violation of the personal integrity of victims, and a serious form of organised crime that threatens the rule of law. although the victims can be of different genders and ages, statistics clearly show that the majority (80%) of victims are women and girls from central and eastern europe. directive 2011/36/eu on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims has established a legal framework for more effective prosecution of traffickers in human beings. the directive calls on member states to integrate the gender dimension into their anti-trafficking initiatives and to provide assistance and support to victims on a case-by-case basis. the report on the directive highlights the inadequate reporting on trafficking in human beings, which indicates inadequate implementation and a lack of political will. the report further calls on member states to increase cooperation in the area of trafficking in human beings, including the identification of potential victims, and highlights the role of eu agencies in the early identification of victims at the borders of the european union. i believe that the report contributes to a strengthened fight against trafficking in human beings, and i have therefore supported it.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the implementation of the directive on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims from the point of view of gender equality. according to the eurostat report on trafficking in human beings, women and girls represent 80% of recorded victims of trafficking in human beings. the worrying figures confirm the thesis that traffickers target the most vulnerable groups of people, who in most cases face a difficult socioeconomic situation. if we are to make a step forward in strengthening the prosecution of organised crime networks that profit from trafficking in human beings, we need to improve the cooperation of the institutions of the european union and the member states. i support strengthening the prosecution of trafficking in human beings in the member states, but this is not enough. in addition to repressive measures, we also need prevention, assistance and protection for victims, training of professionals who deal with these issues and, of course, good crossborder cooperation not only with the member states but also with countries outside the european union. as a society, we must have zero tolerance for human trafficking.
in writing. ‒ i supported the resolution on the debate on cases of breaches of human rights, democracy and the rule of law (rule 135) as eu countries need to make progress in protecting victims of trafficking in human beings, while taking measures to prevent, assist and support victims, especially women. in order to assist victims, it is necessary to ensure that the judiciary, the health system and social services are adequately equipped to detect victims at an early stage and to provide them with follow-up care.
in writing. ‒ i supported the report because i believe it highlights the key problems in preventing trafficking in human beings. it points out that the differences in the laws of the member states facilitate the activities of organised crime, as the risk of prosecution is still too low and the penalties to deter this crime are still insufficient compared to the high profits that can be made. identifying victims, who can be found in a variety of legal and illegal activities, remains one of the most difficult aspects of preventing trafficking in human beings. this requires enhanced cooperation between europol and national law enforcement authorities, additional training for them, the establishment of appropriate support for victims and awareness-raising among the general public about all new forms of trafficking in human beings.
member of the commission. – madam president, i would like to thank the honourable members very much for this discussion. it is always very important that that we hold it and it is also inspiring for the commission, both for myself and my colleagues. you are right that the flow of data from the european union to the united states is really massive. we needed to come forward soon with the new system which will protect the data of european citizens, not because of big companies which have this data flow as a basis for their business, but, as has been mentioned here several times, it was also in the interests of european small and medium—sized enterprises, for which it was a real disaster that they appeared in legal uncertainty. this is just the circumstance which we had to take into account when we worked on this issue after the court ruling – and also before, of course. we needed strong assurances from our american counterparts. we needed to achieve legal certainty and to put an end to uncertainties where the companies were in a very difficult situation. during the negotiations i called our situation and the way we wanted to conclude these negotiations ‘trust and check’. we need to have elementary trust towards our american partners that they will comply with their own laws and that they will do what they have committed themselves to in the official letters signed at the highest possible level. i will share with you today that i cannot say that that privacy shield, as a mechanism to protect eu citizens’ data in the united states, is perfect. it cannot be perfect and i will never be totally satisfied with it, because there were objective reasons why we could not achieve more. one is the matter of the american legal order, which mr albrecht very rightly pointed out here. we do not have any power to change legislation in the united states, but we will keep monitoring developments in this field in the united states and we have expressed many times our conviction that the data will be better protected in america if they have the proper data protection law. we cannot do much more. the second objective, where we could not do more, is access to data for national security purposes. look at the situation in europe. here the commission and the european union does not have any power to ask the secret services to be more transparent and to inform people whether they are using their data or not. not even the member states can do that. certainly we wanted a similar thing when we negotiated the conditions in the united states. so these were our limits. i must say very openly that we are not fully satisfied, but we are satisfied in the sense that we achieved the maximum which was possible. but what is more important is that we must not be satisfied for the future. satisfaction must not be our leading principle for the years to come, because the commission has committed itself – i have committed myself and my colleagues – to monitor on a continuous basis what is happening in the united states. we will do it in a very transparent way through the annual reviews, where we expect all who are to contribute to input the trustworthy data showing the illustration of the situation as it stands, both in the united states and in the european union. i think that this annual review and the very strong suspension clause is quite a strong safeguard and strong measure. i am convinced that we do not need any sunset clause, as has been proposed here. mrs sophie in 't veld is absolutely right that the schrems ruling helped us. i am sorry we waited for it from the moment when we knew that this has been lodged at the court, because we were already convinced before the ruling that the decision would give us proper arguments and proper benchmarks, which will help us negotiate this stronger position. i must say that it helped in the negotiations and we very precisely took article by article in the schrems ruling and we renegotiated in a very tough way with the american partners, referring to the court decision. i cannot be sure that the new court ruling will not be as strict as the previous one, but i am confident that we tailored the privacy shield system on the requirement of the court. so again, we did our best. on the umbrella agreement, i do not know about a situation where we would keep some something secret. there were many written questions, which we answered, to the members of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe). i would like to ask you again not only for your support for the privacy shield but also for the umbrella agreement because, as i said in my opening speech, this is a real improvement in the protection of data in the exchange between law enforcement authorities. we should take into very serious consideration that this is also about the data of witnesses and victims of criminal offences, and this plays an important role in the strengthening of cooperation between the eu and the us in criminal justice and security matters, because we all know that the security situation is worsening and that we will have to do everything we can to have better, swifter and safer cooperation between the law enforcement authorities in the united states and the european union. so i would like to ask you again for your support.
president-in-office of the council. – madam president, honourable members, ladies and gentlemen. first of all, thank you very much for this debate, and thank you to the commission for your clarification about the privacy shield and the further planning. i think this debate makes clear that smooth data flows can never mean uncontrolled and unchecked data flows. the basis of data flows should always be the trust of our citizens that the data are being used in a just and prudent way both in europe and the united states. and if a citizen has the feeling that this is not the case, he or she should be able to object to this use. at the same time we know – and i think that many members have expressed this today – the enormous importance of smooth data flows for governments, companies and american and european citizens, who are reaping the benefits of this. it means companies are being enabled to operate more effectively and efficiently on the european and american side of the atlantic, and therefore we are talking about a very important issue. it also means we will be able to fight crime more effectively and increase the security of both our continents. so we have to see to what extent this can all benefit us, and i think the proposal that has been made is therefore so important. first, on the umbrella agreement. i think – and i refer to many questions that were asked on this – it is important to say that the agreement itself does not constitute a legal basis for the transfer of personal data, it only supplements other agreements with a common set of data protection safeguards. i think that is very important. finally, as you know, the agreement can be suspended in cases where the parties do not live up to it. so that is important. a few questions were raised on the ombudsperson. i think also here we have to underline the fact that the ombudsperson is an additional mechanism compared to other systems. so, in itself, it is not sufficient legal protection. it will not replace more substantive forms of legal protection, and i believe that it is a step forward that the united states has been willing to create this mechanism and trust that the handling of complaints submitted will be conducted in a proper manner. i would like to point out that the ombudsperson does not fulfil its position in isolation but, as stated in annex iii, works in cooperation with the internal regulators of the agencies who will need to provide information and answer questions. i would say that also many eu member states provide for an ombudsperson-type oversight on intelligence activities in our countries. i think, correctly, it was pointed out that the arrest was, if you wish, a catalyst for something that is, i think, a very improved deal. the court was important; it reminded us that an essentially equivalent level of data protection in a third country can only be met if government access to the third country meets the standards of necessity and proportionality. if a third country allows for massive and indiscriminate collection of data, the standards are not met, and in this case the representations by the various us government officials clearly indicated that the us has adopted laws and policies combined with a system of oversight and redress possibilities in order to avoid the massive and indiscriminate collection of data. the main rule is: targeted collection of data, bulk collection, is secondary, and bulk collection, if based on a proper legal standard and with sufficient safeguards to protect the rights and interests of data subjects, is acceptable, since it is not massive and indiscriminate collection of data. then about the ‘sunset clause, i do not want to repeat; i agree with what has been said by the commissioner. i know it is a big point of discussion also in your parliament. i agree in this case with mr voss that we do not need such a sunset clause, since there is a strong element of annual review and monitoring foreseen in the agreement. finally, i would say that we deem that the privacy shield and the umbrella agreement offer the safeguards needed to justify our citizens’ trust. we hope, therefore, also, that the european parliament will consider all the positive aspects. it is also true here to say that the better is the enemy of the good. it is important that we can now make progress on this; it is important for our citizens and our businesses – eu citizens in particular – when consent is given, hopefully to the conclusion of the agreement.
in writing. after the court of justice of the european union declared the safe harbor agreement invalid, the european commission proposed a new regime for data flows between the us and the eu, called the privacy shield. the privacy shield is not intended to be a comprehensive, exhaustive, or exhaustive list of the rights and obligations of the eu and its member states. the commission has also concluded that the contested tax ruling is not in line with the arm's length principle. the agreement also gives comparative advantage to us companies over european companies due to lower requirements compared to eu data protection law. i also believe that there is a possibility that the agreement will be declared invalid in the future, as happened in the case of the safe harbour agreement. in view of all the above, it seems to me reasonable to introduce a time-limit clause which would require the renegotiation and signature of the agreement after a few years, thus allowing for its improvement.

in writing. i strongly support the call on the european commission to assess the impact of the eu minimum income schemes and to consider further action. these measures must include an analysis of the situation and proposals for measures in the field of minimum national pensions, which must not be lower than the poverty threshold. the increasing impoverishment of the elderly population (especially older women) requires immediate action to restore human dignity and a decent quality of life to the elderly poor. the fact that the elderly are labelled as a cost to society, which is a major financial and budgetary problem for local communities, the member states and the european union, is also directly linked to poverty among the older generations. it is therefore the duty of policy-makers to say a firm no to this kind of stigmatisation of the elderly and finally to make decisions that will promote intergenerational respect and ensure a more peaceful old age for today's younger generations. the time has come, ladies and gentlemen, to speak more forcefully about a more binding document aimed at protecting the rights of older people internationally. the call for member states to adopt minimum pension decisions therefore also represents, in my view, an important contribution to the idea that older people are a vulnerable social group whose rights must also be protected at the level of the european union and beyond.

in writing. ‒ i supported the european parliament's motion for a resolution on virtual currencies. seven years after the launch of bitcoin, the first and most important virtual currency, it has become clear that the innovation on which bitcoin is based, the so-called distributed ledger technology (dlt), will have a profound impact on the financial sector and beyond. the main opportunities of virtual currencies and dlt in the area of payments relate to the reduction of transaction costs and ease of use, while ensuring a high level of privacy protection. however, i would point out that the transaction costs for payments are quite high, which means that there is still a lot of work to be done to fully exploit the potential of virtual currencies.
in writing. ‒ seven years after the launch of bitcoin, the first virtual currency, it has become clear that the innovation on which bitcoin is based will have a profound impact on the financial sector and beyond. this technology allows, in principle, a decentralised, fast, robust and fairly secure recording of any transaction together with the history of past transactions in a so-called distributed ledger. while some questions remain regarding the scope of these technological changes, this first european parliament report on virtual currencies and dlt technology comes at the right time because of the significant opportunities and non-negligible risks. the report also takes into account the greens' views on the energy consumption of bitcoin and also our views on the definition of a virtual currency. the report is well balanced and represents a meaningful way forward on virtual currencies, which is why i supported it and voted for its adoption.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on virtual currencies. the virtual currency has been around for seven years, so we can already make a realistic assessment of its impact and its contribution. by reducing transaction and operational costs for payments, reducing the cost of accessing financing without a traditional bank account, increasing the resilience and speed of payment systems and trade in goods and services, virtual currencies can be seen to contribute positively to citizens' well-being and economic development. i therefore support the recommendation to the commission to carry out a comprehensive analysis of virtual currencies and, on the basis of this assessment, to consider amending the current eu legislation on payments, if necessary.
in writing. ‒ i supported the european parliament's motion for a resolution on virtual currencies. virtual currencies will have a greater impact on the financial sector in the future, as they allow for fast and secure transactions. the main advantages of virtual currencies relate to the reduction of transaction costs and ease of use. the risks of using virtual currencies are already apparent today, as they are also used for money laundering and the financing of criminal and terrorist activities. however, it is only when the use of virtual currency becomes more widespread that it will be possible to assess the remaining risks. the supervision of virtual currencies requires the development of sufficient capacities, including in particular technical knowledge. harsh zoning regulations should be avoided, as they could stifle growth. nevertheless, there is a need to regulate this area with immediate and reliable control measures, and thus address risks before they become systemic.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on virtual currencies. i believe that this new technology can offer significant opportunities for the consumer and economic development. however, we have to approach this issue carefully. it innovations can spread very rapidly and become systemic and therefore it is essential that the commission establishes a task force to actively monitor how the technology evolves and to make timely proposals for specific regulation if the need arises.
in writing. - i voted for the report on virtual currencies. virtual currencies and dlt technology can make a positive contribution to the well-being of citizens and economic development, including in the financial sector. this requires the development of a robust legal framework that is in step with innovation and that can respond in a timely and appropriate manner to all risks associated with the use of virtual currencies.

in writing. ‒ i supported the european parliament resolution introducing provisional measures in the field of international protection for the benefit of sweden and italy and greece. these are urgent measures needed to manage the current refugee and migration crisis and to protect european citizens. sweden is facing an emergency situation due to a sudden increase in the number of third-country nationals entering its territory. in 2015, sweden had by far the highest number of applicants for international protection per capita in the eu (11,503 applicants per million inhabitants). by march 2016, sweden had thus accepted a total of 170,104 asylum seekers, of whom 73,331 were children. such figures are significantly too high even for a society as open as sweden's, and therefore the adoption of interim measures in the field of international protection is necessary.

in writing. ‒ the development of the information society and electronic commerce and the improvement of the interception capabilities of intelligence agencies worldwide have increased the flow of data and electronic communications and the risks associated with the misuse of these data. i supported the european parliament's motion for a resolution on the transatlantic flow of data, because such protection would be useless if it were limited to the territory of the union and if, in accordance with the directive, it were not adequately ensured in the third countries to which data are transferred. the eu-us privacy shield reflects the requirements of the judgment of the court of justice of the eu of 6 october 2015, which repealed the previous safe harbour framework. the new arrangement will impose greater obligations on us companies to protect the personal data of europeans and ensure tighter monitoring and enforcement by the us department of commerce and the us federal trade commission, including through enhanced cooperation with european data protection authorities. the new agreement contains an obligation for the us to make the access of public authorities to personal data transferred under the new arrangement subject to clear conditions, restrictions and controls in accordance with us law, in order to prevent pervasive access. europeans will be able to address any queries or complaints to the special new ombudsman.
